captions.text: Welcome to AI Agents with Python, Beginner to Production.
Over this course you will go from writing your first Python data structures to
deploying a full AI agent application with authentication, retrieval, tools, tests,
and monitoring.
This first lesson explains what an agent actually is, how the course works, and then
gets your Python environment ready.
Let's start with a precise definition, because the word agent is used loosely.
An AI agent is a program that is given a goal, not a fixed script.
You describe what you want, for example, research this topic and write me a brief.
The program asks a language model to decide what to do next.
The model does not run anything by itself.
It only returns a decision, as text or as a structured tool request.
Your Python code then performs that action with a tool, such as a web search, a
database query, or a calculator, and feeds the result back to the model.
This repeats in a loop.
Decide, act, observe, and continue, until the goal is reached or a safety limit
stops it.
That loop is the heart of every agent in this course, and you will build it from
scratch in Module 4.
Here is how the eighteen modules fit together.
Part one builds your foundations: Python for AI work, calling language model APIs,
and prompt engineering with validated, structured output.
Part two builds agents from scratch, with no framework hiding the details: the loop,
tool calling, memory, and making agents reliable.
Part three connects agents to knowledge and tools, with the Model Context Protocol,
embeddings, and retrieval-augmented generation.
Part four covers orchestration: LangGraph workflows, multi-agent systems, and web
research agents.
Part five is about quality and security: testing and evaluating agents, and
defending them against prompt injection and data leaks.
And part six takes everything to production, with FastAPI, Docker, monitoring, and a
full-stack AI workspace as the final project.
Every module follows the same rhythm, so you always know where you are.
First, the concepts, explained from zero, with small examples you can run.
Then a real project, built step by step.
Not a teaser.
Complete code, tests, and a README you can run yourself.
Next, the errors people actually hit, and how to fix them.
And finally, a recap, a short quiz with explained answers, and an extension
challenge if you want to go further.
Now, Module 1.
Agents are software, so before we touch a language model, you need the Python that
AI engineering actually uses.
You will work with the core data types, lists, dictionaries, and sets, in the shapes
AI applications use every day.
You will write functions and classes, and handle errors with exceptions.
You will organise code into modules and packages, read and write files and JSON, and
keep settings in environment variables.
And you will add type hints, make HTTP requests, and get a first, practical look at
async and await.
Everything comes together in this module's project, the Python AI Toolkit.
It is a command line tool that reads a log of language model API calls, validates
every record, and produces a report.
Here is the finished tool.
The validate command checks every record and explains exactly what is wrong, like a
negative token count, or a missing id.
And the report command summarises a clean log: requests, success rate, tokens,
estimated cost, and latency.
By the end of this module, you will have written every line of it.
To follow along you need a computer running Windows, macOS, or Linux.
You need Python 3.11 or newer.
I am recording with Python 3.13.
A code editor.
VS Code with the official Python extension is a good free choice.
And no AI experience at all.
If you have written a little code in any language, that helps, but every concept is
explained as we go.
Let's set up a clean workspace.
Open a terminal in an empty folder.
First, check your Python version.
On Windows the command is usually just python, or py.
Anything from 3.11 up is fine.
Next, create a virtual environment.
This makes a private folder, called dot venv, with its own copy of Python and its
own installed packages.
Every project gets one, so the libraries of one project can never break another.
Activate it.
On macOS and Linux, use source, dot venv, slash bin, slash activate.
On Windows, run dot venv, backslash Scripts, backslash activate.
Now, the python command points inside your project folder.
With the environment active, pip installs packages into it.
We install httpx, the HTTP library we will use later in this module, and we pin the
exact version, so that your results match mine.
Finally, pip freeze records the exact versions you installed into a requirements
file.
Anyone can rebuild the same environment with pip install, dash r, requirements dot
text.
One warning.
If pip complains about an externally managed environment, or packages seem to
vanish, you are almost certainly outside your virtual environment.
Activate it again, and check that which python, or where python on Windows, points
into your project folder.
This is the project layout we will grow into by the end of the module.
At the top: the virtual environment, which is never committed to git, a settings
template, and the pinned requirements.
Configuration and sample data live in their own folders.
The real code lives in a package called toolkit.
The special file dunder main lets us run the whole package with python dash m
toolkit.
And tests live in their own folder.
Keeping code, data, configuration, and tests separate is a habit that pays off in
every AI project you build.
An agent is a program that decides, acts, observes, and repeats, working towards a
goal.
The model only decides.
Your Python code performs the actions.
Every project gets its own virtual environment, with pinned versions.
In the next lesson, we write real Python: the data types that every AI application
is built from.
See you there.
